questions.question_text:
After an outlier is removed from a set of advertising spend and monthly sales data, the line of best fit has a steep, positive gradient.
The removed outlier had low spend but unusually high sales.
What can you conclude about the line of best fit BEFORE the outlier was removed?

options.text: It was less steep than the line after removal, because the outlier pulled its low-spend end upward.
It was steeper than the line after removal, because more data points usually mean a steeper line.
options.why: The number of points doesn't determine steepness — where the extra point sits relative to the trend does.

options.text: It had a negative gradient, because a high-sales, low-spend point suggests spending doesn't help sales.
options.why: One point being unusual doesn't establish the direction of the whole dataset's trend.

options.text: It was identical to the line after removal, because a line of best fit ignores individual outliers.
options.why: A line of best fit is fitted using every point, including outliers, so an outlier does affect it.

questions.solution_text:
A low-spend, high-sales outlier sits above where the trend of the rest of the data would put it.
Including it pulls the low-spend end of the line upward, flattening the line compared to the trend of the remaining points.
So the original line, with the outlier included, must have been less steep than the steep line seen after its removal.
